rows.branch: All branches (the Arya Samaj is reported to treat only the four Saṃhitās as revealed and the Upanishads as authoritative where they agree with them; not verified)
rows.reference: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1 (the closing section of the Upanishad)
rows.original: ahiṃsan sarvabhūtāny anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ (a variant reads ahiṃsant; Böhtlingk's emendation of one word is noted in the secondary source)
rows.says: A householder who studies the Veda, raises virtuous sons, draws all his senses into the Self and never gives pain to any creature, except at the tīrthas, and lives so all his life, reaches the world of Brahman and does not return.
rows.bearing: A wider duty not to harm any creature (sarvabhūtāni), so it reaches every person K1 protects, newborns and outsiders included (rule 7, rule 9). It therefore teaches K1 and K0 through the wider rule. The exception 'except at the tīrthas' is usually read as occasions that scripture itself enjoins, chiefly sacrifice (animals, exclusion e); Śaṅkara's gloss was not verified here. If it is read as 'whatever scripture permits', it also covers courts and war (exclusions a and b, context only, rule 5). No reading found makes it cover a private person killing a person on his own authority; human victims are expressly released in the one Vedic rite that names them (see Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.6.2.13). The reach of the exception is the one open point.
rows.strength: Explicit (wider rule); reach of the exception not fully resolved
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): sacred-texts.com SBE 1, page 'VIII, 15', showing 'never giving pain to any creature, except at the tîrthas' and the no-return outcome; Sanskrit confirmed through a Jain scholarly page on jainqq.org (not on the project's list)

rows.reference: Bhagavad Gita 16.1 to 3, especially 16.2 (= Mahabharata critical ed. 6.38.1 to 3; Ganguli, Bhishma Parva Section XL)
rows.original: ahiṃsā satyam akrodhas tyāgaḥ śāntir apaiśunam / dayā bhūteṣv aloluptvaṃ mārdavaṃ hrīr acāpalam
rows.translation: Swami Swarupananda (1909); Telang (SBE 8) not seen for these verses
rows.says: Among the marks of one born to the divine nature are non-injury, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, calm, no slander, compassion to beings, freedom from greed, gentleness and modesty. The same chapter sets these against the demonic marks of pride, anger and harshness.
rows.bearing: Teaches a wider duty of non-injury and compassion towards all beings, reaching everyone K1 protects (rule 7), so it teaches K1 and K0 through the wider rule. Absence of anger and of greed bears directly on K0's motives. It is taught as a character to cultivate, not as a rule, hence Clear teaching. The same book tells Arjuna to fight; that is war, context only (rule 5).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): sacred-texts.com, Swarupananda, Sixteenth Chapter, verse 2 list confirmed ('Non-injury, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, tranquillity, absence of calumny, compassion to beings, un-covetousness, gentleness, modesty, absence of fickleness')

rows.reference: Bhagavad Gita 16.14, read in its passage 16.13 to 15 (= Mahabharata critical ed. 6.38.14)
rows.original: asau mayā hataḥ śatrur haniṣye cāparān api
rows.says: The demonic person, deluded by ignorance, says: 'That enemy has been slain by me, and others also shall I slay. I am the lord, I enjoy, I am successful, powerful and happy.' The Gita gives this as the outlook of those bound for ruin.
rows.bearing: Presents killing one's enemies out of pride, desire and enmity as the mark of the demonic nature, to be shunned. This teaches K0 (no killing out of hatred, revenge or for one's own gain) at the Clear teaching level. On its own it does not reach K1's full wording (rule 7), which rests on the wider-rule rows. The related verses 16.19 (the cruel and hateful cast into demonic births) and 16.21 (desire, anger and greed as the three gates of hell) would strengthen this but were not verified (search budget exhausted).

rows.reference: Bhagavad Gita 13.7 (13.8 in editions that number Arjuna's opening question; = Mahabharata critical ed. 6.35.7; Ganguli, Section XXXVII)

rows.says: Humility, lack of pretence, non-injury, forbearance and uprightness head the list of qualities called 'knowledge'; Swarupananda's note says they are so called because they lead to knowledge.
rows.bearing: A second, independent statement in the Gita of non-injury as a required quality of the seeker, reaching all beings (rule 7). Supports K1 and K0 through the wider rule.

rows.reference: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.6.2.13 (Mādhyandina recension; Eggeling, SBE 44, XIII, 6, 2)
rows.original: puruṣamedha (name of the rite); Sanskrit of the verse not checked
rows.says: In the human sacrifice, the human victims have fire carried round them but are not yet slaughtered when a voice says: 'Puruṣa, do not consummate these victims: if you did, man would eat man.' He sets them free and makes the offerings instead.
rows.bearing: Within Tier 1, a voice in the text forbids killing the human victims and gives a reason that applies to all people. So the one Vedic rite that names human victims is not left as approval of killing persons, which removes a possible contradiction of K1 (rule 2 not met). It protects a named class in one setting, so on its own it is 'taught in part' (rule 7); it strengthens the reading of Chāndogya 8.15.1 that its exception does not cover persons. Scholars report that some later ritual manuals describe the rite differently (not verified).

rows.reference: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13 to 18 (pañcikā 7, adhyāya 3; Haug's 'VII, 3'): the story of Śunaḥśepa
rows.translation: Not seen in the original; narrative as summarised by J. Eggeling (introduction to SBE 44) and a wisdomlib study of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
rows.says: King Hariścandra has vowed his son to the god Varuṇa. The son buys the boy Śunaḥśepa from his starving father Ajīgarta for a hundred cows as a substitute. When no one will bind or kill the boy, Ajīgarta does both for further hundreds of cows. The boy prays to the gods and is freed. Viśvāmitra condemns Ajīgarta as not having left the ways of a Śūdra and his deed as irremediable, and the boy rejects him as having done what is unknown even among Śūdras.
rows.bearing: The text condemns a father's readiness to kill his own child for gain, which supports K0 (no killing for one's own gain) and K1's protection of children against a parent, as Clear teaching through story. Limit: the frame presupposes that a god demanded a human sacrifice and accepted a substitute. The killing is not carried out and the text approves neither the demand nor the killer (rule 4); whether the god's acceptance counts as approval is for the counter-evidence search (rule 6 at most).
rows.strength: Clear teaching, borderline (for K0; condemnation seen only in secondary summaries)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), secondary only: the sale, the binding, the father's offer to kill and the condemnation confirmed through Eggeling's introduction (wisdomlib.org) and a wisdomlib study ('The Legend of Śunaḥśepa'); the Aitareya text itself was not seen

rows.reference: Brahma Sūtra 3.1.25 with Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya
rows.original: aśuddham iti cen na śabdāt; the rule is quoted as na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni (form as commonly cited; not checked)
rows.says: An objector says sacrifices are impure because they injure animals, citing the scriptural rule 'Do not harm any creature'. Śaṅkara answers that right and wrong are known from scripture alone: the rule is a general one, and the specific injunction to offer an animal to Agni and Soma is an exception to it.
rows.bearing: Shows the classical tradition treating 'harm no creature' as a general scriptural rule that yields only to a specific scriptural injunction. The exception discussed concerns animals (exclusion e). Supports reading the Tier 1 ahiṃsā texts as a binding wider rule (rule 7); the commentary is Tier 2 and reconciles only. Note: no extant Vedic source for the quoted rule was traced in this research; the nearest verified Tier 1 text is Chāndogya 8.15.1.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (Tier 2, reconciling); the Sūtra itself is Implied for K1

support.reconciliation: Hinduism has no single body that rules for the whole tradition, so each reconciliation binds only the schools that accept it. (1) Revealed scripture (śruti: the Vedas with their Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas and Upanishads) outranks remembered tradition (smṛti: the epics and law books) where they conflict: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.3.3 as cited by Śaṅkara, Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya 2.1.1 (classical commentator, Tier 2 for reconciliation; verified in earlier research). So law-book rules on graded penances or a wide right to kill assailants yield to the Tier 1 duty not to harm any creature (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1) where they conflict. (2) General rule and specific exception: Śaṅkara on Brahma Sūtra 3.1.25 (verified) treats 'do not harm any creature' as a general scriptural rule that only a specific scriptural injunction can set aside; the exception he discusses is animal sacrifice (outside K1). (3) The one Vedic rite that names human victims, the puruṣamedha, has the victims released before they are killed, because 'man would eat man' (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.6.2.13, Tier 1, verified); the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa's Śunaḥśepa story condemns the father who would kill his son for cows (verified only through secondary summaries). (4) War and royal punishment are assigned to the ruler and the warrior class as their own duty (Bhagavad Gita 2.31 to 38; Manusmṛti 7; neither verified here); these are outside K1. Self-defence against an assailant (ātatāyin) is permitted in the law books (Manusmṛti 8.348 to 351, Tier 2, not verified). (5) Rites to harm enemies (the Atharvaveda's hostile charms, the śyena rite) are held by Mīmāṃsā (Śabara on Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2) to be described, not approved, because injury is forbidden: reported in Article I, not verified. (6) Metaphysical verses saying the Self neither kills nor is killed (Kaṭha 1.2.19, Gita 2.19, 18.17) and that the knower is untouched by any deed (Kauṣītaki 3.1) are read by Śaṅkara as about the Self or the knower who acts without ego, not as licence to kill: not verified. Standing: Śaṅkara binds Advaita only; Rāmānuja's and Madhva's readings of these verses were not searched; Mīmāṃsā is a classical school not listed in corpus.md.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule), provisional pending the counter-evidence search
K1.reason: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1 (Tier 1, all branches, verified) explicitly makes not harming any creature part of the path, which reaches every person K1 protects (rule 7, rule 9); the Bhagavad Gita states the same duty three times (16.2, 13.7, 17.14, verified, Clear teaching). The 8.15.1 exception ('except at the tīrthas') is read as scripturally enjoined occasions, chiefly animal sacrifice (exclusion e) and possibly courts and war (exclusions a and b); Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.6.2.13 releases the human victims of the only rite that names them. No verified counted text found by this search permits a private killing of a person. The label could become Unclear (rule 6) if the counter researcher confirms and cannot reconcile Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.10.3 (girls 'put aside' at birth, disputed), Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1 (the knower untouched by killing) or the Atharvaveda's hostile charms (killing by sorcery, possibly defensive).

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Taught through the wider rule (Chāndogya 8.15.1; Gita 16.2, 13.7, 17.14) and directly at Clear teaching level: Gita 16.2 names absence of anger and greed among the divine marks, and Gita 16.14 gives 'that enemy has been slain by me, and others also shall I slay' as the speech of the demonic nature (verified). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa's condemnation of a father ready to kill his son for cows supports it (secondary verification only). Tier 2 adds Manusmṛti 4.164 (no striking in anger) and Mahabharata 13.114.8, which support only.

K3.label: Silent in counted texts (provisional); taught in Tier 2, unverified
K3.reason: No Tier 1 text on sparing non-combatants was found; the Gita's call to fight (war context, rule 5) concerns combatants and says nothing about non-combatants. Explicit rules sparing those who surrender, the unarmed, the sleeping, fugitives and onlookers are recalled from Manusmṛti 7.90 to 93, Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.5.10.11 and Mahabharata 6.1.27 to 32, all Tier 2 (not counted) and not verified in this session.

rows.branch: Schools that accept Manusmṛti. Its authority is contested: the Arya Samaj accepts it only where it agrees with the Vedas, and anti-caste movements reject it (corpus.md)
rows.reference: Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 (Bühler numbering; the Sanskrit editions seen agree for 11.33)
rows.original: vāk śastraṃ vai brāhmaṇasya tena hanyād arīn dvijaḥ (11.33)
rows.says: A Brahmin who knows the law need not take a wrong to the king. By his own power he may punish those who injure him, because his power is greater than the king's. He may use the Atharva Veda spells without hesitation: speech is the Brahmin's weapon, and with it he may slay his enemies.
rows.bearing: The hardest verified text. If counted, it would contradict K1 and K0 (rules 2 and 5): it lets a private person, outside the king's court, kill those who have already wronged him. That is retaliation, not defence against an attack under way, and it is a privilege of one class only. But it is Tier 2 and contested, so it does not decide a label (rule 1). Open points: whether killing by spell counts as deliberate killing (the law books treat lethal sorcery as a real offence; see the next row), and how Medhātithi reads the verse (not seen). The rule that revealed scripture outranks the law books would set it aside if a Tier 1 text forbids it. But the Atharva Veda itself contains spells against enemies (see the Atharva Veda row, unverified).

The tradition's own classical reading (next row) holds that the Veda states the means for whoever wants the result, but does not enjoin it as right conduct (dharma), and that the act is a wrong. rows.reference: Śabara, Mīmāṃsā Sūtra Bhāṣya on 1.1.2 (locus recalled, not confirmed)
rows.original: na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni (the general prohibition, recalled)
rows.says: Mīmāṃsā authors treat the śyena, a Vedic rite to kill an enemy, as something that should not be done. The Veda states it as a means for whoever desires to harm, but harming is forbidden, so the rite is harmful (anartha) and not right conduct (dharma).
rows.bearing: This is the tradition's own classical way of reading Vedic sorcery texts: describing a means is not approving it. It turns any verified abhicāra or śyena text from a possible contradiction into, at most, Unclear (rule 6). Standing: Śabara (about the 5th century) is the foundational commentator of Mīmāṃsā, the school whose rules govern how Dharmaśāstra reads the Veda.

rows.says: Fire has been carried round the bound human victims, but they have not been slaughtered, when a voice tells the sacrificer not to complete the rite: if he did, man would eat man. The victims are released, and offerings are made to the same gods instead.

rows.reference: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13 to 18 (the Śunaḥśepa story; reference recalled)
rows.translation: M. Haug (1863) or A. B. Keith, HOS 25 (1920); neither seen
rows.says: As recalled: King Hariścandra vows his son to the god Varuṇa as a sacrifice. The son escapes and buys a Brahmin boy, Śunaḥśepa, from his father Ajīgarta for a hundred cows. The father takes more cows to bind the boy and to kill him himself. Śunaḥśepa praises the gods, his bonds fall away, and he is freed. He reproaches his father for taking up the knife, and the sage Viśvāmitra adopts him.
rows.bearing: A parent willing to kill his own child for payment, at a king's rite that a god demanded. If verified, the story reports this without approving it: the killing never happens, the victim is freed by the gods, and the father is rebuked (rule 4, Implied). The god's demand within the story makes it a hard case, which could be Unclear under rule 6 rather than simply silent. Unverified, so it decides nothing (rule 1).

rows.reference: Manusmṛti 11.127 in Bühler = 11.126 in some Sanskrit editions
rows.original: vaiśye 'ṣṭamāṃśo vṛttasthe śūdre jñeyas tu ṣoḍaśaḥ
rows.says: The penance for killing a Kṣatriya is a quarter of the penance for killing a Brahmin. For a Vaiśya it is an eighth, and for a Śūdra a sixteenth. Bühler writes 'virtuous Śūdra', but in the Sanskrit 'of good conduct' goes with the Vaiśya. The next verses give lighter penances for unintentional killing.
rows.bearing: Graded protection (rule 2): the killer's guilt depends on the victim's class. It is not a permission, because every such killing still needs expiation. It limits equal protection under K1 and K0 but does not contradict them. Tier 2, not counted (rule 1). The king's punishment is a separate matter (context: court). rows.reference: Manusmṛti 8.348 to 351 (Bühler numbering)
rows.original: ghnan dharmeṇa na duṣyati (8.349)
rows.says: Twice-born men may take up arms when their duties are obstructed. Whoever kills rightly in self-defence, in a fight over the priests' fees (dakṣiṇā), or to protect women and Brahmins incurs no guilt (8.349). As recalled, 8.350 to 351 add that one may kill without hesitation an attacker (ātatāyin) who comes to kill, even a teacher, a child, an old man or a learned Brahmin, without guilt.
rows.bearing: Self-defence and the defence of women fall within the exception in K1 and K0, so this does not contradict them (rule 7). Two parts go further. 'A fight over fees' goes beyond the exception if it means killing to keep property; commentators may read it as defence against armed robbers, but that was not checked. The rescue of Brahmins is singled out by status. Tier 2, not counted (rule 1).

rows.reference: Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra 3.15 to 18 (Bühler, SBE 14; numbering recalled)
rows.original: ṣaḍ ete hy ātatāyinaḥ (recalled)
rows.says: As recalled: six kinds of person are 'attackers' (ātatāyin): the arsonist, the poisoner, the man with a weapon in his hand, the robber, and whoever seizes another's land or wife. Whoever kills an attacker who comes intending to kill, even one learned in the Veda, incurs no guilt.
rows.bearing: If the permission covers all six kinds, it allows blameless killing of robbers and land-takers, which goes beyond the exception in K1 and K0 (killing or grave harm). If, as the wording 'intending to kill' suggests, it covers only those coming to kill, it stays within the exception. Tier 2 and unverified, so it decides nothing (rule 1).

rows.reference: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1 (recalled)
rows.original: ahiṃsan sarvabhūtāny anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ
rows.says: As recalled: the Upanishad ends by describing the person who learns the Veda, keeps a household and studies, harming no living being except at the tīrthas, and reaches the world of Brahman. Śaṅkara is recalled as glossing tīrthas as the cases that scripture allows.

On the commentators' reading the exception covers what scripture allows: animal sacrifice (exclusion e), and, on some readings, lawful punishment and war (a and b). It gives no licence for private killing. If verified, it is Clear teaching (wider rule) for K1 and K0, and the rule that revealed scripture outranks the law books would set it above Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33. Unverified, so it decides nothing.

rows.reference: Ṛg Veda 10.18.7 to 8 (parallel: Atharva Veda 18.3.1 to 2)
rows.original: ud īrṣva nāry abhi jīvalokam (10.18.8)
rows.says: In a funeral hymn, wives whose husbands are living come forward with ointment (v. 7). Then the dead man's wife, lying by his side, is told to rise and come back to the world of the living, because he is lifeless (v. 8).
rows.bearing: The Vedic funeral hymn calls the widow back to life and gives no ground for widow-burning (sati). Later defenders of sati are recalled as reading agneḥ ('of fire') for agre ('first') in verse 7; that reading is unverified. Atharva Veda 18.3.1 is recalled as describing the wife lying down beside the dead 'keeping an ancient custom' before she is raised (unverified). This is the Tier 1 answer to the Tier 2 sati texts. Sati itself is presented as the widow's own act, so it falls under exclusion (d); a forced burning would be a killing that no counted text was found to approve.

counter.reconciliation:
Hinduism has no single authorised body that rules for the whole tradition, so each reading binds the schools that accept it. Its own reconciliation of hard texts on killing runs as follows.

(1) Rank of texts. Revealed scripture (śruti: the Vedas with Brāhmaṇas and Upanishads) outranks remembered tradition (smṛti: law books, epics, Purāṇas). Where they conflict, the law book is set aside (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.3.3, cited by Śaṅkara, Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya 2.1.1). This is a classical rule used across the Vedānta schools, verified earlier as annex row HI-13. It subordinates Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33, the hardest verified text, to any Tier 1 duty of non-injury. corpus.md also records that Manusmṛti's authority is contested within the tradition (the Arya Samaj, Gandhi, Ambedkar).

(2) Describing a means is not approving it. In Mīmāṃsā, the classical school that governs how Dharmaśāstra reads the Veda, the śyena rite for killing an enemy is the standard case. The Veda states the means for whoever wants the result, but harming is forbidden, so the rite is harmful and not dharma. This is attributed to Śabara on Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2 (about the 5th century, the school's foundational commentator), but his own words were not verified; a secondary source confirms that Mīmāṃsā authors agree the śyena should not be done. The same reading would apply to the Atharva Veda spells against enemies, which are unverified in this run.

(3) The Brāhmaṇas reconcile their own hard narratives. In the human sacrifice the victims are released and a voice forbids killing them (Śatapatha 13.6.2.13, verified). In the Śunaḥśepa story the boy is freed and his father rebuked (unverified).

(4) Sati. The Ṛg Veda's funeral hymn calls the widow back to the living (10.18.8, verified). Medhātithi (about the 9th to 10th century) condemned a widow's self-immolation as forbidden suicide, while Vijñāneśvara and Aparārka supported it (verified only through a secondary book). The classical authorities were split, and the matter falls under exclusion (d).

(5) Graded penances are expiations, not permissions. Every killing in the law books needs penance, scaled by the victim's class (Manusmṛti 11.127, verified). Manu also treats lethal sorcery as a punishable wrong (9.290 and 11.64, unverified), which narrows 11.31 to 33 to a Brahmin's privilege against those who injure him. No classical commentary on 11.33 was read.

(6) Defence. Killing an attacker who comes to kill is blameless (Manusmṛti 8.349, verified; 8.350 to 351 and Vasiṣṭha 3.15 to 18, unverified). This matches the exception in K1 and K0, except where it reaches fights over fees or robbers of land and goods.

(7) War. The Gita (Tier 1) presents fighting a righteous war as a warrior's duty. The law books and the epic (Tier 2) forbid killing those who surrender, the unarmed, onlookers, women, children and the old (unverified, apart from a weak sighting of Baudhāyana's wording).

Standing: śruti texts are counted (Tier 1). Śaṅkara, Śabara and Medhātithi are classical authorities used for reconciliation (Tier 2). Modern reformers such as Rammohun Roy, Gandhi and Ambedkar are outside the corpus and were not checked in this run.

K1.label: Taught (provisional and borderline); not contradicted in the counted texts verified
K1.reason: Rule 1: no verified Tier 1 text permits, commands or approves a deliberate killing that K1 forbids. The verified Tier 1 hard texts point the other way: the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa forbids killing the human victims of its own rite (13.6.2.13), and the Ṛg Veda's funeral hymn calls the widow back to life (10.18.8). The clearest verified text against K1 is Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33. It lets a Brahmin, on his own authority and without the king, slay with Atharva Veda spells those who injure him, which would contradict K1 under rules 2 and 5. But it is Tier 2 and contested, so it does not decide. Graded penances (Manusmṛti 11.127) are graded protection, not permission (rule 2). 'Taught' rests on Tier 1 support outside this hunt: Gita 6.32 is verified but borderline Clear teaching (wider rule); Gita 16.2 and Chāndogya 8.15.1 are unverified. Hence 'borderline'. If the Atharva Veda spells against enemies, the Ṣaḍviṃśa śyena injunction or the Śunaḥśepa story are verified, they bear directly on K1. The tradition's own Mīmāṃsā reading and the story's own release of the victim narrow them, so the likely result would then be Unclear (rule 6), not Contradicted.

K0.label: Taught (provisional and borderline); not contradicted in the counted texts verified
K0.reason: The same verified evidence applies. Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 (Tier 2, not counted) is retaliation against those who have injured a Brahmin, so it would contradict K0 if counted. The Atharva Veda refrain against 'him who hates us and whom we hate' would bear directly on K0's 'hatred' clause, but it is unverified and is a petition to the gods (rule 4), so the likely result if verified is Unclear (rule 6). The strongest Tier 1 support, Gita 16.12 to 18 condemning those who kill enemies out of desire, anger and pride, is unverified in this run. The verified wider rule (Gita 6.32) is borderline, so the result stays provisional.

K3.label: Silent in counted texts (provisional); taught in Tier 2, not counted
K3.reason: The Tier 1 texts on war (Gita 2.31 to 38; the Ṛg Veda hymns on Indra's wars) neither protect nor target non-combatants as far as recalled (both unverified in this run), and divine war deeds are Implied (rule 4). Protection of non-combatants is taught in Tier 2: Manusmṛti 7.90 to 93 (those who surrender, sleep, are unarmed, onlookers, fleeing), Baudhāyana (women, children, old men, except attackers) and the Mahabharata's condemnation of Aśvatthāman's night massacre. None of these is verified to the standard, and none is counted (rule 1).

Over each offering he says that he takes away the lover's breath, sons, cattle, sacrifices and good works, and hopes. The man cursed by a brahmin who knows this departs from this world without strength and without merit.

It gives a husband, acting on his own authority and out of hatred, a rite to make a man who threatens no one's life 'depart from this world'. If it is verified, and 'departs from this world' (asmāl lokāt praiti) means death, and death by such a rite counts as deliberate killing, it bears directly on K0 (hatred, revenge) and on K1 (a husband's private act). rows.reference: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13 to 18 (pañcikā 7, adhyāya 3; Haug's 'VII, 3'): the story of Śunaḥśepa
rows.translation: M. Haug (1863) or A. B. Keith, HOS 25 (1920); neither seen. The narrative was seen only as summarised by J. Eggeling (introduction to SBE 44) and in a wisdomlib study
rows.says: King Hariścandra has vowed his son to the god Varuṇa. The son buys the boy Śunaḥśepa from his starving father Ajīgarta for a hundred cows, as a substitute. When no one else will, Ajīgarta binds the boy and takes up the knife to kill him for more cows. The boy prays to the gods and is freed. Viśvāmitra condemns Ajīgarta's deed, the boy rejects his father, and Viśvāmitra adopts him.
rows.bearing: Two sides. The story condemns a father who would kill his child for gain, which supports K0 and K1's protection of children. But its frame has a god demanding a human sacrifice and accepting a substitute, and a king who intends to give his son. The killing is never carried out and the would-be killer is condemned (rule 4). The god's acceptance of a victim makes it a hard case. It is a ritual killing, not a judicial punishment, so exclusion (a) would not obviously cover it. If verified at the primary-text level, the likely result is Implied for support and, at most, Unclear (rule 6) as counter-evidence.

rows.reference: Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 (Bühler numbering)
rows.original: vāk śastraṃ vai brāhmaṇasya tena hanyād arīn dvijaḥ (11.33)
rows.says: A brahmin who knows the law need not take a wrong to the king. By his own power, which is greater than the king's, he may punish those who injure him. He may use the Atharvaveda spells without hesitation: speech is the brahmin's weapon, and with it he may slay his enemies.
rows.bearing: The hardest verified text. If counted, it would contradict K1 and K0 (rules 2 and 5): it lets a private person, outside the king's court, kill those who have already wronged him. That is retaliation, not defence, and it is a privilege of one class. It is Tier 2 and contested, so it does not decide (rule 1). The rule that revealed scripture outranks the law books would set it aside against a Tier 1 duty of non-injury, and Manu itself fines lethal sorcery (9.290, unverified) and makes non-injury the first common duty (10.63, unverified). It also reads the Atharvaveda as supplying such spells, which is why the Tier 1 sorcery leads matter. No classical commentary on 11.33 was read.

verified.reconciliation: Hinduism has no single body that rules for the whole tradition, so each reconciliation binds the schools that accept it. (1) Rank of texts. Revealed scripture (śruti: the Saṃhitās, Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas and Upanishads) outranks remembered tradition (smṛti: law books, epics, Purāṇas) where they conflict. The authority is Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.3.3, cited by Śaṅkara, Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya 2.1.1, a classical rule used across the Vedānta schools (project record HI-13, VERIFIED (search); attribution worth one direct reading). It subordinates Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33, the hardest verified text, to the Tier 1 duty of non-injury (Chāndogya 8.15.1; Gita 16.2, 13.7, 17.14). corpus.md also records that Manusmṛti's authority is contested within the tradition. The rule cannot reach Tier 1 texts themselves. (2) General rule and specific exception. Śaṅkara on Brahma Sūtra 3.1.25 treats 'do not harm any creature' as a general scriptural rule that only a specific scriptural injunction sets aside. The exception he discusses is animal sacrifice, outside K1 (VERIFIED (search) by the support researcher, not re-checked). (3) Describing a means is not approving it. Mīmāṃsā, the school whose rules govern how Dharmaśāstra reads the Veda, holds that the śyena rite for harming an enemy is stated as a means but is not dharma, because injury is forbidden (Śabara on Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2; UNVERIFIED, seen only through a secondary source). This is the tradition's own way to read the Tier 1 sorcery texts (Atharvaveda rites, the śyena injunction, and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 if verified). It also shows that the tradition counts such rites as real injury by the performer. (4) The Brāhmaṇas settle their own hard narratives. In the human sacrifice the victims are released because 'man would eat man' (Śatapatha 13.6.2.13, VERIFIED (search) by both researchers). In the Śunaḥśepa story the boy is freed and the father condemned (UNVERIFIED; secondary summaries only). (5) Graded penances are expiations, not permissions (Manusmṛti 11.127, VERIFIED (search) on sites not on the project's list). Manu also fines lethal sorcery (9.290, UNVERIFIED) and makes non-injury the first duty of all classes (10.63, UNVERIFIED to standard). (6) Defence. Killing an attacker who comes to kill is blameless (Manusmṛti 8.349 VERIFIED (search); 8.350 to 351 and Vasiṣṭha 3.15 to 18 UNVERIFIED). This matches the exception in K1, except possibly the 'fight over fees' and robbers of land or goods. (7) War and royal punishment belong to the ruler and the warrior (Gita 2.31 to 38, Manusmṛti 7; UNVERIFIED) and are outside K1. The law books and the epic forbid killing those who surrender, the unarmed, onlookers, women, children and the old (all Tier 2, UNVERIFIED). (8) Widow-burning: the Ṛg Veda funeral hymn calls the widow back to life (10.18.8, VERIFIED (search)), and Medhātithi condemned the practice as forbidden self-killing while later commentators supported it (secondary source only). It falls under exclusion (d). Standing: śruti texts are counted (Tier 1). Śaṅkara, Śabara and Medhātithi are classical authorities used to reconcile (Tier 2); Śaṅkara's readings bind Advaita only, and Rāmānuja's and Madhva's readings of the hard verses were not checked. Modern reformers (Rammohun Roy, Gandhi, Ambedkar) are outside the corpus and were not checked.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule), provisional
K1.reason: This rests on rows the support researcher verified by search, none of which this verifier could re-check (search budget used up before any search ran). Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1 (Tier 1, Explicit, wider rule) and Bhagavad Gita 16.2, 13.7 and 17.14 (Tier 1, Clear teaching, wider rule) teach not harming any being. That reaches every person K1 protects, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). No verified counted text permits, commands or approves a private killing of a person. The one Vedic rite naming human victims releases them (Śatapatha 13.6.2.13). The verified Atharvaveda counter-charm (10.1) aims at sorcerers whose witchcraft is attacking, which the verifier reads as within the defence exception on the hymn's own terms; if the project instead treats any lethal counter-sorcery as a hard case, rule 6 gives Unclear, and the draft should say which reading it takes. The hardest verified text, Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33, is Tier 2 and contested, so it does not decide (rule 1). Open point: the reach of 'except at the tīrthas' in 8.15.1 (Śaṅkara's gloss not seen). Risks to the label are all unverified Tier 1 leads: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (a husband's rite, out of hatred, to make his wife's lover 'depart from this world'), the śyena injunction, the Atharvaveda rites against enemies, Kauṣītaki 3.1, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.10.3 and the Śunaḥśepa story. If they are verified, the likely result is Unclear (rule 6). Contradicted is possible if Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 is verified, no classical reading narrows it, and the project counts killing by rite as deliberate killing. Under a strict reading of the verifier's instruction (only rows this check itself confirmed count), no row would count and the label would be 'not decided'. That is not Silent, because the texts exist but are unconfirmed.

K0.label: Taught, provisional
K0.reason: Taught through the same wider-rule rows (rule 7). It is also taught directly at Clear teaching level: Gita 16.2 names freedom from anger and from greed among the divine marks, and Gita 16.14 gives 'that enemy has been slain by me, and others also shall I slay' as the speech of the demonic nature to be shunned (verified by search by the support researcher; not re-checked). Tier 2 adds Manusmṛti 4.164 (no striking anyone in anger) and Mahabharata 13.114.8, which support only. The same caveat on re-checking applies. K0 is more exposed than K1 to Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12, which names hatred as the motive. If that verse is verified it would likely make K0 Unclear (rule 6), or Contradicted if unnarrowed and if killing by rite counts as killing. The Atharvaveda refrain against 'him who hates us and whom we hate' (unverified) is a petition, so Implied (rule 4). Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 (retaliation by spell) is Tier 2 and does not decide.

K3.label: Silent in counted texts (provisional)
K3.reason: No verified Tier 1 text either protects or targets non-combatants. The Gita's call to fight (2.31 to 38, unverified) concerns combatants in an agreed battle. The Ṛg Veda hymns on Indra's wars are a god's deeds and petitions (rule 4) and are unverified. Tier 1 war texts were barely searched (the Atharvaveda battle charms not at all), so this silence is weakly established. Explicit protection of those who surrender, the unarmed, sleepers, onlookers, fugitives, women, children and the old is recalled from Manusmṛti 7.90 to 93, Āpastamba 2.5.10.11, Baudhāyana 1.10.18.11 and Mahabharata 6.1.27 to 32, with the Sauptika Parva's condemnation of a night massacre. All of these are Tier 2 (not counted, rule 1), and none is verified to the standard.

verified.branch_notes: All rows that decide the provisional labels (Chāndogya 8.15.1; Gita 16.2, 16.14, 13.7, 17.14) are Tier 1 texts that the four main denominations (Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, Smārta) all accept, so no label currently depends on a single branch. The Brāhmaṇa rows (Śatapatha 13.6.2.13, Aitareya, Ṣaḍviṃśa) depend on accepting the Brāhmaṇas as revealed. The Arya Samaj is reported (not verified) to accept only the four Saṃhitās as revealed and the Upanishads only where they agree with them. Under METHOD.md section 9, decision 3, it is probably a reform movement rather than a branch (standard reference works list the four denominations as the main divisions), but this has not been decided. If it were a branch, its counted texts would be the Saṃhitās. The only verified Saṃhitā row (Atharvaveda 10.1) is a counter-charm, and the Saṃhitā support (Atharvaveda 10.1.29, Īśa Upaniṣad 6 as Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 40) is unverified, so its K1 and K0 results would be Silent or Unclear (rule 3). Śaiva Siddhānta gives primacy to the Āgamas, which are not in corpus.md, and Vīraśaiva or Lingāyat strands that reject Vedic authority were not considered; both are unchecked branch questions. Classical readings: Śaṅkara binds Advaita only; Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and Madhva (Dvaita) readings of Chāndogya 8.15.1, Gita 18.17, Kauṣītaki 3.1 and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 were not checked. The Mīmāṃsā reading of the śyena is used across Dharmaśāstra but is unverified. Manusmṛti and the other law books are accepted in varying degrees, and their authority is contested (corpus.md); none of them decides a label.
verified.fairness_notes: 1. Verification asymmetry. This verifier could not run a single search, so Hinduism's rows were not independently re-checked, while other traditions' verifiers may have had searches. Dropping the researchers' search-verified rows for that reason alone would turn a budget failure into a substantive verdict ('Silent'), judging Hinduism more strictly than others. They are therefore kept as VERIFIED (search), clearly marked as not re-checked, and the labels are marked provisional. A follow-up check should be run before the article is drafted. 2. Sorcery and curses. If killing by rite or curse counts as deliberate killing against Hinduism (Atharvaveda rites, the śyena, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12), the same rule must apply to curses and imprecations in other traditions. Examples, not checked in this run: Elisha's curse followed by the deaths of the youths at 2 Kings 2:23 to 24 (Judaism and Christianity), and imprecatory prayers such as Psalm 109. Prayers asking God or gods to destroy an enemy should get the same rule 4 treatment everywhere. Hindu tradition is distinctive only in that it explicitly classifies some rites as the performer's own act of injury, and in fairness that same tradition also forbids them (Mīmāṃsā). 3. Tier rule. Placing the Mahabharata and the law books in Tier 2 (METHOD.md section 9, decision 4) makes Hinduism Silent on K3, although its classical rules of fair war (dharmayuddha) are among the most developed of any tradition. In traditions whose secondary texts are treated as primary (for example the Sunnah), similar rules count. The same placement also shields Hinduism from its hardest texts (Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33, the Paraśurāma story). Both effects should be reported, so the tier rule is not seen as favouring or penalising the tradition. 4. Style of teaching. Hinduism's Tier 1 texts state non-injury mainly as a virtue to cultivate (the Gita's lists) and as the closing rule of an Upanishad, not as a law code, so Clear teaching is the right rating and consistent with Article I. Readers should not take the absence of a Decalogue-style rule as weakness. 5. Translation. Bühler renders varṇa as 'caste', which can make status-graded texts (Manusmṛti 11.127, 8.380) read more starkly than the Sanskrit (translations.md). 6. No single authority. Śaṅkara's readings bind Advaita only and should not be presented as 'the Hindu view'. Modern Hindu rejection of Manusmṛti (the Arya Samaj, Gandhi, Ambedkar) is real but outside the corpus, so it cannot reconcile counted texts; this cuts both ways and should be said plainly.
